t: Count Substrings With Every Vowel and Exactly K Consonants
o: Count substrings containing all five vowels and exactly k consonants. In 'aeioqq', k=1 there are none; in 'aeiou', k=0 the whole string qualifies once; in 'ieaouqqieaouqq', k=1 three substrings qualify. Since n ≤ 250, an O(n^2) brute force passes, but the elegant solution converts 'exactly k' into 'at least k minus at least k+1', each countable with a two-pointer window.
k: exactly(k) = atLeast(k) - atLeast(k+1); each atLeast count is computable with a sliding window because validity is monotone under shrinking.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute Force Over All Substrings
a.i: Fix the left endpoint, extend right while consonant count ≤ k, and record a hit whenever all five vowels are present and consonants equal k. With n ≤ 250 this is at most ~31k steps.
s: For each left index i, maintain a vowel counter and consonant count.
Extend j to the right; stop early once consonants exceed k.
Add 1 whenever all five vowels appear and consonants == k.
a.t: O(n^2) — each of the n left endpoints scans at most n characters.
a.sp: O(1) — the vowel counter holds at most five keys.

a.i: Define f(K) = number of substrings containing all five vowels and at least K consonants. For each right endpoint, shrink the window from the left while it remains valid; afterwards, left points at the first invalid start, so exactly 'left' valid substrings end at r. Validity (all vowels present, consonants ≥ K) is preserved by shrinking, so two pointers work. Answer = f(k) - f(k+1).
s: Write f(K) using a window with a vowel map and consonant counter.
For each r, add the character; while the window is valid, remove word[left] and advance left.
Add left to the result (number of valid starts for this r).
a.t: O(n) per call to f, two calls total — each pointer moves monotonically.

w: The at-least/at-least-plus-one difference is the standard way to convert 'exactly k' into a two-pointer-friendly condition. Pitfalls: off-by-one in the shrink loop (after shrinking, l is the first INVALID start, so add l, not l+1), and handling k = 0 correctly (the condition cons >= 0 is vacuous). Follow-up: the hard version with n up to 5e4 requires exactly this O(n) technique.
